stem: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is defined as __________.
options: The market value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic territory of a country during a year
The total value of only agricultural goods
The income earned by citizens abroad
solution: GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT (GDP) is the MARKET VALUE of ALL FINAL GOODS and SERVICES PRODUCED WITHIN the DOMESTIC TERRITORY of a country during a YEAR (an accounting period). It measures production located inside the country, regardless of whether the producers are nationals or foreigners. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The three methods of measuring national income (GDP) are the product (value added) method, the income method and the __________ method.
solution: The THREE METHODS of measuring NATIONAL INCOME are: the PRODUCT (VALUE ADDED) method (sum of value added by all producing units), the INCOME method (sum of factor incomes — rent, wages, interest, profit), and the EXPENDITURE method (sum of final expenditures — C + I + G + net exports). All three give the same total because output = income = expenditure. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Value added' by a firm is calculated as __________.
options: Value of output minus the value of intermediate goods (inputs) used
Value of output plus intermediate goods
solution: VALUE ADDED by a firm = VALUE of OUTPUT − VALUE of INTERMEDIATE GOODS (inputs purchased from other firms). It measures the firm's OWN contribution to output, avoiding double counting. Summing value added across all firms gives GDP by the product method. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The problem of 'double counting' in measuring national income is avoided by __________.
options: Counting only the value of final goods, or only the value added at each stage
Adding intermediate and final goods together
solution: DOUBLE COUNTING (counting the value of a good more than once as it passes through stages of production) is AVOIDED by either counting ONLY the value of FINAL GOODS, or by summing the VALUE ADDED at EACH STAGE (which excludes the value of intermediate inputs). Both approaches give the same, correct total. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The difference between GDP and GNP (Gross National Product) is __________.
options: Net factor income from abroad (GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad)
solution: The difference between GDP and GNP is NET FACTOR INCOME from ABROAD (NFIA): GNP = GDP + NFIA. NFIA is the factor income earned by a country's NATIONALS ABROAD minus the factor income earned by FOREIGNERS within the country. GDP is production-based (domestic territory); GNP is nationality-based. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Net factor income from abroad (NFIA) is __________.
options: Factor income earned by residents from abroad minus factor income earned by non-residents within the country
solution: NET FACTOR INCOME from ABROAD (NFIA) = factor income earned by a country's NORMAL RESIDENTS from ABROAD − factor income earned by NON-RESIDENTS (foreigners) WITHIN the country's domestic territory. It is the item that converts 'domestic' aggregates to 'national' aggregates. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Net' aggregates are obtained from 'Gross' aggregates by subtracting __________.
solution: NET aggregates are obtained from GROSS aggregates by SUBTRACTING DEPRECIATION (consumption of fixed capital). For example, NET Domestic Product (NDP) = GDP − Depreciation, and Net National Product (NNP) = GNP − Depreciation. Depreciation is the capital used up in production. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The difference between 'market price' and 'factor cost' aggregates is __________.
options: Net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies)
solution: The difference between MARKET PRICE and FACTOR COST valuations is NET INDIRECT TAXES (NIT) = INDIRECT TAXES − SUBSIDIES. Aggregate at FACTOR COST = Aggregate at MARKET PRICE − NET INDIRECT TAXES. Market price includes taxes (and excludes subsidies); factor cost reflects what factors of production actually receive. So option 1 is correct.

stem: National Income is technically defined as __________.
options: Net National Product at factor cost (NNP at FC)
Gross National Product at market price
solution: NATIONAL INCOME is technically defined as NET NATIONAL PRODUCT at FACTOR COST (NNP at FC) — i.e., the sum of factor incomes (rent, wages, interest, profit) earned by a country's normal residents, net of depreciation and valued at factor cost. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In the expenditure method, GDP (at market price) equals C + I + G + __________.
options: Net exports (exports minus imports, X − M)
solution: By the EXPENDITURE method, GDP at market price = C (private final CONSUMPTION expenditure) + I (INVESTMENT / gross capital formation) + G (GOVERNMENT final consumption expenditure) + NET EXPORTS (EXPORTS − IMPORTS, i.e., X − M). This sums all final expenditure on domestically produced goods and services. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Nominal GDP' (GDP at current prices) differs from 'Real GDP' (GDP at constant prices) in that nominal GDP __________.
options: Is valued at current-year prices and can rise merely because prices rise, while real GDP uses base-year (constant) prices to remove the effect of price changes
Is measured in a foreign currency
solution: NOMINAL GDP (GDP at CURRENT PRICES) is valued at the PRICES of the CURRENT year, so it can RISE merely because PRICES RISE (inflation), even if output is unchanged. REAL GDP (GDP at CONSTANT/BASE-YEAR PRICES) values output at fixed base-year prices, REMOVING the effect of price changes, so it reflects the true change in the volume of output. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP (multiplied by 100) is called the __________.
solution: The GDP DEFLATOR = (NOMINAL GDP ÷ REAL GDP) × 100. It is a broad measure of the GENERAL PRICE LEVEL of all goods and services included in GDP, and is used to gauge inflation across the whole economy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Real GDP is considered a better indicator of economic growth than nominal GDP because it __________.
options: Reflects changes in the actual quantity of goods and services produced, not just price changes
solution: REAL GDP is a BETTER INDICATOR of economic GROWTH because it REFLECTS CHANGES in the ACTUAL QUANTITY (volume) of goods and services produced — it is measured at constant prices, so it is NOT inflated by mere PRICE CHANGES. A rise in real GDP means genuinely more output, indicating true growth. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Personal Income' is derived from National Income by making adjustments such as __________.
options: Subtracting undistributed profits, corporate taxes and net interest paid by households, and adding transfer payments
solution: PERSONAL INCOME (income actually received by households) is derived from NATIONAL INCOME by SUBTRACTING income earned but not received — UNDISTRIBUTED (retained) PROFITS, CORPORATE (profit) TAXES, and net interest paid by households — and ADDING income received but not currently earned, chiefly TRANSFER PAYMENTS (pensions, subsidies, etc.). So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Personal Disposable Income' is obtained from Personal Income by subtracting __________.
options: Personal (direct) taxes and other compulsory payments (like fines)
solution: PERSONAL DISPOSABLE INCOME (PDI) = PERSONAL INCOME − PERSONAL (DIRECT) TAXES − other compulsory payments/miscellaneous receipts of government (like fines and fees). It is the income households actually have available to SPEND or SAVE. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Transfer payments' (like old-age pensions, scholarships, and unemployment allowances) are NOT included in national income because __________.
options: They are receipts for which no goods or services are produced/rendered in return (no value added)
They are too small to matter
solution: TRANSFER PAYMENTS (old-age PENSIONS, SCHOLARSHIPS, unemployment allowances, gifts) are NOT included in national income because they are RECEIPTS for which NO GOODS or SERVICES are PRODUCED or rendered in RETURN — there is NO VALUE ADDED. They merely transfer purchasing power from one party to another and are not payment for current production. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Why is GDP not a fully adequate measure of economic welfare?
options: It ignores distribution of income, non-market activities, externalities (pollution), and the composition of output
It counts only welfare and no production
solution: GDP is NOT a fully adequate measure of WELFARE because it IGNORES: the DISTRIBUTION of INCOME (a high GDP may still mean many poor people); NON-MARKET activities (like unpaid household work); EXTERNALITIES such as POLLUTION and environmental damage (which may even raise GDP while reducing well-being); and the COMPOSITION of output (e.g., more weapons vs. more food). So GDP growth need not mean higher welfare. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Externalities, such as pollution from a factory, are a limitation of GDP as a welfare measure because __________.
options: GDP does not deduct the harm (negative externalities) that production imposes on others, so it can overstate welfare
solution: EXTERNALITIES like POLLUTION are a limitation because GDP does NOT DEDUCT the HARM (NEGATIVE EXTERNALITIES) that production imposes on OTHERS — e.g., a factory that pollutes a river adds its output to GDP but the damage to health and environment is not subtracted. Thus GDP can OVERSTATE actual welfare. So option 1 is correct.

stem: If real GDP rises but the distribution of income becomes more unequal, then __________.
options: Overall welfare may not improve for the majority, even though total output is higher
Inequality has no effect on welfare
solution: If REAL GDP RISES but income DISTRIBUTION becomes MORE UNEQUAL, then OVERALL WELFARE may NOT IMPROVE for the MAJORITY — the extra output might accrue mainly to a few rich people while most people gain little. This shows why GDP alone, ignoring distribution, is an incomplete welfare measure. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In the income method, national income is the sum of factor incomes: compensation of employees, rent, interest, and __________.
options: Profit (and mixed income of the self-employed)
solution: By the INCOME METHOD, domestic income is the sum of FACTOR INCOMES: COMPENSATION of EMPLOYEES (wages/salaries), RENT (and royalty), INTEREST, and PROFIT — plus MIXED INCOME of the SELF-EMPLOYED (income of own-account workers combining wages, rent, interest, and profit). Adding NFIA gives national income. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Compensation of employees' includes wages and salaries in cash and kind plus __________.
options: Employers' contributions to social security schemes (like provident fund)
solution: COMPENSATION of EMPLOYEES includes: WAGES and SALARIES in CASH and in KIND (benefits), plus EMPLOYERS' CONTRIBUTIONS to SOCIAL SECURITY schemes (such as provident fund, pension, and insurance). It is the total reward for labour. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The value of production for self-consumption (e.g., farmers consuming their own produce) is __________ in national income.
options: Included (imputed at market value), because it is part of current output
Excluded, because no money changes hands
solution: The value of production for SELF-CONSUMPTION — e.g., FARMERS consuming their OWN PRODUCE — IS INCLUDED in national income, IMPUTED (estimated) at MARKET VALUE, because it is PART of CURRENT OUTPUT even though no market transaction occurs. Excluding it would understate the economy's true production. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The imputed rent of owner-occupied houses is __________ in national income.
options: Included, because the house provides a housing service that has value
Excluded, because the owner pays no rent
solution: The IMPUTED RENT of OWNER-OCCUPIED HOUSES IS INCLUDED in national income, because the house provides a valuable HOUSING SERVICE (the owner effectively 'pays rent to themselves'). If it were excluded, two identical houses — one rented, one owner-occupied — would be treated differently, understating output. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is NOT included in the estimation of national income?
options: Sale of second-hand goods and purely financial transactions (like buying old shares)
solution: The SALE of SECOND-HAND GOODS (already counted when first produced) and purely FINANCIAL TRANSACTIONS (like buying/selling OLD SHARES and bonds, which merely transfer ownership) are NOT included in national income, as they involve NO new PRODUCTION. Newly produced goods and current services ARE included. So option 1 is correct.

stem: GDP at market price minus net indirect taxes equals __________.
solution: GDP at MARKET PRICE − NET INDIRECT TAXES (indirect taxes − subsidies) = GDP at FACTOR COST. Removing net indirect taxes converts a market-price valuation into a factor-cost valuation, reflecting what the factors of production actually earn. So option 1 is correct.

stem: If a country's NFIA (net factor income from abroad) is negative, then __________.
options: Its GNP is less than its GDP
Its GNP is greater than its GDP
solution: Since GNP = GDP + NFIA, if NFIA is NEGATIVE (foreigners earn more factor income within the country than the country's residents earn abroad), then GNP is LESS than GDP. This is common in economies with large foreign investment whose profits flow out. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'circular flow' basis of national income accounting implies that the three methods (product, income, expenditure) should __________.
options: Yield the same total national income, since output equals income equals expenditure
solution: Because output = income = expenditure in the CIRCULAR FLOW, the THREE METHODS of measuring national income — PRODUCT (value added), INCOME, and EXPENDITURE — should YIELD the SAME TOTAL national income. In practice small statistical discrepancies arise, but conceptually all three are equal. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following would INCREASE a country's real GDP?
options: An increase in the actual quantity of goods and services produced
A rise in prices with output unchanged
An increase in second-hand car sales
solution: REAL GDP increases only when the ACTUAL QUANTITY (volume) of goods and services PRODUCED rises. A mere rise in PRICES (with output unchanged) raises nominal but not real GDP; second-hand sales and transfer payments do not represent new production, so they do not add to real GDP. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The value of intermediate goods is not separately added in GDP. Reason (R): GDP counts only final goods (or value added) to avoid double counting. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — the value of INTERMEDIATE GOODS is NOT separately added in GDP. R is TRUE and correctly EXPLAINS A: GDP counts only FINAL GOODS (or equivalently, VALUE ADDED at each stage) precisely to AVOID DOUBLE COUNTING, since the value of intermediate goods is already embodied in final goods. So R is the correct explanation of A. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which correctly orders these aggregates from largest to smallest (typically), assuming positive depreciation and net indirect taxes?
options: GDP at MP → NDP at MP → NDP at FC (national income concepts follow by adjusting NFIA)
NDP at FC → NDP at MP → GDP at MP
solution: Typically, GDP at MARKET PRICE is the LARGEST; subtracting DEPRECIATION gives NDP at MARKET PRICE (smaller); subtracting NET INDIRECT TAXES gives NDP at FACTOR COST (smaller still). (Corresponding NATIONAL concepts are obtained by adding NFIA.) So the descending order is GDP at MP → NDP at MP → NDP at FC. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The base year in real GDP calculation is used because __________.
options: It provides a fixed set of prices to value output across years, so changes reflect quantity not price
It is the year GDP was invented
It is always the current year
solution: The BASE YEAR is used in REAL GDP calculation because it provides a FIXED SET of PRICES (constant prices) at which output of different years is valued. This way, CHANGES in real GDP reflect changes in the QUANTITY of output, NOT changes in PRICES — allowing meaningful comparison of production over time. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Non-monetary (non-market) exchanges, like unpaid domestic services by homemakers, are generally __________ in official national income.
options: Excluded (or under-recorded), which is a limitation of GDP
solution: NON-MONETARY (non-market) exchanges, such as the UNPAID DOMESTIC SERVICES of HOMEMAKERS, are generally EXCLUDED (or under-recorded) in official national income because they are not bought and sold in the market and are hard to value. This is a recognised LIMITATION of GDP as a measure of true economic activity and welfare. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Domestic territory' of a country for national accounting includes __________.
options: The political frontiers plus ships/aircraft operated by residents, embassies abroad, and fishing vessels/oil rigs operated by residents
solution: The DOMESTIC TERRITORY of a country, for national accounting, includes the area within its POLITICAL FRONTIERS, PLUS: SHIPS and AIRCRAFT operated by RESIDENTS between countries; EMBASSIES, consulates, and military bases located ABROAD; and FISHING VESSELS, OIL RIGS, and floating platforms operated by residents in international waters. It excludes foreign embassies located within the country. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'normal resident' of a country is a person or institution that __________.
options: Ordinarily resides in the country and whose centre of economic interest lies in that country
Is merely a tourist visiting for a week
Is a foreign diplomat posted in the country
solution: A NORMAL RESIDENT is a person (or institution) who ORDINARILY RESIDES in a country and whose CENTRE of ECONOMIC INTEREST lies in that country. It EXCLUDES foreign tourists, foreign diplomats and officials, and international organisation staff. Residence, not citizenship, is the key criterion for 'national' income. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The consumer price index (CPI) differs from the GDP deflator in that the CPI measures __________.
options: The change in prices of a fixed basket of goods and services consumed by a typical household
Prices of all goods produced in the economy
solution: The CONSUMER PRICE INDEX (CPI) measures the CHANGE in PRICES of a FIXED BASKET of GOODS and SERVICES CONSUMED by a TYPICAL HOUSEHOLD. The GDP DEFLATOR, by contrast, covers ALL goods and services produced in the economy (including capital goods and government services). So the CPI focuses on consumption; the deflator on total output. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Gross Domestic Capital Formation (investment) consists of gross fixed capital formation and __________.
solution: GROSS DOMESTIC CAPITAL FORMATION (gross investment) consists of GROSS FIXED CAPITAL FORMATION (additions to fixed assets — machinery, buildings, etc.) PLUS the CHANGE in STOCKS (INVENTORY INVESTMENT — the change in stocks of raw materials, semi-finished, and finished goods). So option 1 is correct.

stem: In the expenditure method, 'net exports' being negative means that __________.
options: Imports exceed exports (a trade deficit), reducing GDP measured by expenditure
solution: NET EXPORTS = EXPORTS − IMPORTS. If net exports are NEGATIVE, then IMPORTS EXCEED EXPORTS (a TRADE DEFICIT). Since imports are goods produced abroad, they are subtracted, so negative net exports REDUCE the GDP figure obtained by the expenditure method. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a DIRECT tax (relevant to converting personal income to disposable income)?
solution: A DIRECT TAX is levied directly on income or wealth and borne by the same person — e.g., INCOME TAX (and corporate tax, wealth tax). SALES tax/GST, EXCISE duty, and CUSTOMS duty are INDIRECT taxes (levied on goods/services, shifted to consumers). Personal disposable income is found by subtracting direct (personal) taxes from personal income. So option 1 is correct.

stem: An INDIRECT tax (which creates a gap between market price and factor cost) is exemplified by __________.
options: Goods and Services Tax (GST) / excise duty
solution: INDIRECT TAXES are levied on goods and services and raise their MARKET PRICE above FACTOR COST — examples include GST, EXCISE DUTY, and CUSTOMS DUTY. INCOME tax, CORPORATE tax, and WEALTH tax are DIRECT taxes. Net indirect taxes (indirect taxes − subsidies) are what separate market-price and factor-cost aggregates. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A subsidy on a good has the effect of making its __________.
options: Market price lower than its factor cost
Market price higher than factor cost
solution: A SUBSIDY (a government payment to producers to lower prices) makes a good's MARKET PRICE LOWER than its FACTOR COST — the factors of production receive more (through the subsidy) than the price consumers pay reflects. This is why NET indirect taxes = indirect taxes − subsidies when moving between market-price and factor-cost valuations. So option 1 is correct.

stem: If nominal GDP rises from one year to the next but real GDP stays the same, we can conclude that __________.
options: The rise is entirely due to an increase in prices (inflation), not in output
solution: If NOMINAL GDP RISES while REAL GDP stays the SAME, the ENTIRE rise must be due to an INCREASE in PRICES (INFLATION), not in the quantity of output. Real GDP unchanged means the volume of goods and services produced did not change; only their money value rose. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Per capita income' (per capita national income) is calculated as __________.
options: National income divided by the total population
solution: PER CAPITA INCOME (per capita national income) = NATIONAL INCOME ÷ TOTAL POPULATION. It is a rough measure of the average income and standard of living per person, and is often used (as real per capita income) to compare living standards across countries or over time. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Two countries can have the same GDP but very different levels of welfare because of differences in __________.
options: Population size, income distribution, non-market activity, and environmental quality
solution: Two countries with the SAME GDP can have very different WELFARE because of differences in POPULATION SIZE (affecting per capita income), INCOME DISTRIBUTION (equal vs. unequal), the extent of NON-MARKET activity, and ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY (pollution not deducted from GDP). These factors, ignored by raw GDP, strongly affect actual well-being. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The windfall gain from a lottery or the sale of an old painting is NOT part of national income because __________.
options: It does not correspond to any current production of goods or services
It is a form of investment
solution: A WINDFALL GAIN (like a LOTTERY prize) or the sale of an OLD PAINTING is NOT part of national income because it does NOT correspond to any CURRENT PRODUCTION of goods or services. Lottery winnings are a transfer, and reselling an old asset merely changes ownership — neither adds new value to the economy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In the value-added (product) method, the sum of gross value added of all sectors gives __________.
options: Gross Domestic Product at market price (or factor cost, depending on valuation)
solution: In the VALUE-ADDED (PRODUCT) method, summing the GROSS VALUE ADDED of ALL producing SECTORS (primary, secondary, tertiary) gives GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT — at MARKET PRICE or FACTOR COST depending on the valuation used. This is one of the three equivalent ways of measuring domestic output. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly states an identity in national income accounting?
options: NNP at FC (National Income) = GDP at MP − Depreciation − Net Indirect Taxes + Net Factor Income from Abroad
National Income = GDP at MP + Depreciation
National Income = GDP at MP + Net Indirect Taxes
solution: A correct identity is: NATIONAL INCOME (NNP at FACTOR COST) = GDP at MARKET PRICE − DEPRECIATION (to get net) − NET INDIRECT TAXES (to get factor cost) + NET FACTOR INCOME from ABROAD (to get national from domestic). Each adjustment converts one aggregate concept to the next. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'expenditure', 'income', and 'product' methods are also called, respectively, measuring national income at the phases of __________.
solution: The three methods correspond to three PHASES of the circular flow: the PRODUCT method measures at the PRODUCTION phase (value generated), the INCOME method at the DISTRIBUTION phase (income distributed to factors), and the EXPENDITURE method at the DISPOSITION phase (income spent on final goods). All three capture the same flow at different points. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Green GNP / Green accounting is proposed to correct conventional national income by __________.
options: Accounting for environmental depletion and degradation, giving a more sustainable measure of income
solution: GREEN GNP (green accounting) is proposed to CORRECT conventional national income by ACCOUNTING for ENVIRONMENTAL DEPLETION (using up natural resources) and DEGRADATION (pollution) — subtracting these costs to give a more SUSTAINABLE measure of income that reflects whether growth is achieved without depleting the natural resource base. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which institution is responsible for estimating India's national income (GDP)?
options: The National Statistical Office (NSO), earlier the Central Statistical Organisation (CSO)
The Reserve Bank of India alone
solution: India's NATIONAL INCOME (GDP) is estimated by the NATIONAL STATISTICAL OFFICE (NSO) — earlier known as the CENTRAL STATISTICAL ORGANISATION (CSO) — under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. It compiles the national accounts using the product, income, and expenditure methods. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'National Income Accounting' is that:
options: NATIONAL INCOME ACCOUNTING measures an economy's output/income through related aggregates — GDP (final goods produced within the domestic territory), GNP (GDP + net factor income from abroad), and their NET (minus depreciation) and FACTOR-COST (minus net indirect taxes) versions, with NATIONAL INCOME being NNP at factor cost; it can be measured by three equivalent methods — PRODUCT (value added), INCOME, and EXPENDITURE — that avoid double counting; REAL GDP (at constant prices) rather than nominal GDP measures true growth, and the GDP DEFLATOR gauges the price level; but GDP has LIMITATIONS as a welfare measure, ignoring income distribution, non-market activities, and externalities like pollution
solution: The chapter's overall message is that NATIONAL INCOME ACCOUNTING measures an economy's OUTPUT and INCOME through a family of related AGGREGATES: GDP (the market value of FINAL goods and services produced WITHIN the DOMESTIC TERRITORY), GNP (= GDP + NET FACTOR INCOME from ABROAD), and their NET versions (subtracting DEPRECIATION) and FACTOR-COST versions (subtracting NET INDIRECT TAXES) — with NATIONAL INCOME defined as NNP at FACTOR COST. It can be measured by THREE EQUIVALENT METHODS — the PRODUCT (VALUE ADDED), INCOME, and EXPENDITURE methods — which, by counting only final goods or value added, AVOID DOUBLE COUNTING and yield the same total (output = income = expenditure). REAL GDP (at CONSTANT prices), not NOMINAL GDP, measures TRUE GROWTH, and the GDP DEFLATOR gauges the general price level. However, GDP has important LIMITATIONS as a measure of WELFARE — it ignores the DISTRIBUTION of income, NON-MARKET activities (like unpaid domestic work), and EXTERNALITIES such as POLLUTION — so a rising GDP does not automatically mean higher well-being. So the overall message is option 2.
